clue.text: Conserving energy, got old motor a metal fan

indicators.note: something conserving another holds it safe inside, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: had means got, as in 'had a letter'
E is the physics symbol for energy
a banger is British slang for an old, battered car

explanation.surface: Someone saving fuel buys a decrepit car from a heavy-metal enthusiast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conserving' puts the energy inside 'got'. 'Motor' is British slang for a car, and an old one is a banger; the 'fan' is a person, not a cooling device.
explanation.definitionFit: A headbanger is a heavy-metal devotee, named for the violent head-shaking done at gigs.

clue.text: Cut in crime affecting a PC

definitions.meaning: an illegal break-in to a computer system

explanation.surface: A cutback in cybercrime hitting home computers.
explanation.walkthrough: PC here is a personal computer, not a police constable.
explanation.definitionFit: Hack is both to chop at something and an unauthorised intrusion into a computer.

clue.text: Agassi's first return of service is some way off

indicators.note: the first letter of the tennis player's name is taken
a return goes back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: Andre Agassi's return of a serve lands far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' and 'service' are tennis terms in the surface; RAF is the Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: Afar means at a great distance, far away.

clue.text: Brighton going wild with fine time guys come out

indicators.note: going wild means running riot, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: A night in Brighton when the town goes wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going wild' mixes BRIGHTON with FINE. Guys are effigies of Guy Fawkes, burnt on 5 November in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonfire Night, 5 November, is when British crowds burn effigies called guys.

clue.text: Indefinite number above number that's lower

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece above another comes first

parts.note: n stands for an unspecified number in maths
ether is something that numbs, an old anaesthetic

explanation.surface: A mathematical statement about one number being placed over another.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'number' is read as 'numb-er', a thing that numbs: ETHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Nether is an adjective meaning lower or under, as in nether regions.

clue.text: Some corn, though wanting filling loaf for a snack

parts.note: an ear is a head of corn, part of the crop

indicators.note: lacking its filling means the inner letters are gone, only the ends kept

parts.note: loaf, as in 'use your loaf', is the head, and nut is slang for it too

explanation.surface: Someone peckish without a bread filling, settling for corn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting filling' leaves TH from 'though'. 'Loaf' is Cockney slang for head (loaf of bread), which is also a nut.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthnut is another name for the peanut, a common snack.

clue.text: Onion, or what people do when cutting one back

indicators.note: going back means the word is read from its end to its start

parts.words: what people do when cutting one
parts.note: chopping an onion makes people cry, and to blub is to weep

explanation.surface: A kitchen musing on onions and the tears they draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns BLUB, the British informal word for weeping, round. 'one' refers back to the onion of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An onion is a bulb, the swollen underground storage organ of the plant.

clue.text: Prosaic fellow interrupting criminal in court

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking in, so this piece goes into the middle of the other
criminal suggests something wrong or bent, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: man means a fellow or chap

explanation.surface: A dull man heckles a defendant during a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges IN COURT to UNROTIC, and 'interrupting' puts MAN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Unromantic means matter-of-fact and lacking sentiment, just as prosaic does.

clue.text: Ruler therefore in poor area is the cause of rising

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, here splitting the outer word

parts.note: bad means poor in quality
a king is a ruler
so means therefore

explanation.surface: A monarch in a deprived region, and the cause of an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: The rising is a cake's, not a rebellion's.
explanation.definitionFit: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated, making dough and batter rise.

clue.text: Hot drink coming in future retail outlet

parts.note: cha is an old British word for tea
what is in store lies ahead, in the future

explanation.surface: A shop promising that a hot drink will be on sale soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming' is only a link word. 'In store' means awaiting us, the future.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain store is one shop in a group under common ownership, a type of retail outlet.

clue.text: Some hiker tramps around in this

definitions.text: Some hiker tramps around in this

indicators.note: turned around means the run of letters is read from right to left
some of the phrase means only part of its letters are taken, a run spanning the words

explanation.surface: A hiker tramping about on a long walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes KERT from 'hiker tramps' and 'around' turns it round; the whole clue also describes a trek.
explanation.definitionFit: A trek is a long arduous journey on foot, just what a tramping hiker undertakes.

clue.text: Scrap Bronte's puerile work about mistreated cat

parts.note: a ding-dong is British slang for a fight or heated row, a scrap
the Bronte sisters published under the pen-name Bell: Currer, Ellis and Acton

explanation.surface: A reader rubbishes a juvenile Bronte piece about animal cruelty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puerile' means for children here: the work is a nursery rhyme, where pussy is put in the well.
explanation.definitionFit: Ding Dong Bell is the nursery rhyme in which a cat is thrown down a well.

clue.text: Most of his arm hurt with vaccine number two

indicators.note: hurt means damaged or injured, so these letters are knocked into a new order
most of a word is all but its last letter, so the final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone's arm is sore after a second vaccine jab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' cuts 'his' to HI; 'hurt' shuffles HI, ARM and VACCINE. 'number two' reads as a second dose but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice-chairman is deputy to the chair, second in command of a board or committee.

clue.text: Not the high-fliers among Ronald Reagan or JFK's staff?

definitions.text: Not the high-fliers among Ronald Reagan or JFK's staff?

parts.words: Not the high-fliers among Ronald Reagan or JFK's staff?
parts.note: Ronald Reagan and JFK are names of US airports, whose workers who stay on the tarmac do not fly

explanation.walkthrough: The presidents look like the point, but Ronald Reagan Washington National and JFK are airports; their non-flying staff work on the tarmac.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground crew are the airport workers who service aircraft but stay on the ground.

clue.text: Like, perhaps, Bengali food for which you may be charged

definitions.text: for which you may be charged

parts.note: Bengali is an Indic language, so something like it is Indic
table means the food served, as in 'keeps a good table'

explanation.surface: A restaurant bill for Bengali cuisine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' suggests a bill but means accused of a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: An indictable offence is one for which a person can be formally accused and tried.

clue.text: Park employee's 4x4 car over leaves

indicators.note: leaves means departs, so this word goes out of the longer one

parts.note: the Range Rover is a well-known British four-wheel-drive vehicle

explanation.surface: A park warden's off-roader is parked under fallen leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' is a verb here, not foliage: OVER departs from RANGE ROVER. The 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranger is a warden who looks after a national park or forest.

clue.text: Silly me, admitting grand acts of theft

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: muggins is a self-mocking British term for oneself as a fool
G is short for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A rueful confession to stealing a large sum.
explanation.walkthrough: MUGGINS, British slang for 'silly me', admits G, a grand.
explanation.definitionFit: Muggings are street robberies, attacks made in order to steal from the victim.

clue.text: Daughter feeling it's a step down

parts.note: an emotion is a feeling

explanation.surface: A daughter feels moving out is a comedown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' is a link meaning the result is.
explanation.definitionFit: A demotion lowers someone to a lesser rank, a move downward in status.

clue.text: Person who exploits freak 1-1 result

indicators.note: a freak result is an unexpected fluke, so the letters come out twisted into a new order

parts.note: each 1 is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A football draw described as a fluke score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freak' rearranges II with RESULT.
explanation.definitionFit: A utiliser makes use of something, putting it to practical or profitable advantage.

clue.text: Cook coq au vin or duck, say, to go in cooler

parts.note: to do food is to cook it, as in 'done to a turn'

parts.words: coq au vin or duck, say
parts.note: both are poultry dishes, examples of bird on the menu

explanation.surface: Kitchen instructions to cook a poultry dish and chill it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooler' is slang for prison, not a fridge; 'do bird' is British slang for serving a jail sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To do bird is British slang for serving time in jail, and the cooler is slang for prison.

clue.text: Gag outspoken rascal

indicators.note: outspoken here means spoken out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: to retch is to gag, heave as if to vomit

explanation.surface: Silencing a cheeky rogue who speaks his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a muzzle or joke, but is a verb meaning heave.
explanation.definitionFit: A wretch is a scoundrel or rogue, often affectionately said.

clue.text: Beer guts?

parts.note: guts means bravery, and beer can lend a drinker false bravery

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beer guts' looks like paunches; read 'guts' as nerve, courage that comes from drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch courage is boldness gained from drinking alcohol rather than real bravery.

clue.text: Lush yellow in orchard hedges

indicators.note: the phrase hedges, or encloses, the letters inside it

explanation.surface: Verdant yellow plants border an orchard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' is a noun, a drunkard, not luxuriant growth.
explanation.definitionFit: A lush is slang for a heavy drinker, as is a wino.

clue.text: Different university that's gone online?

parts.note: e- is the prefix for electronic, online versions of things
the LSE is the London School of Economics, part of the University of London

explanation.surface: Asking whether a university that moved online has changed.
explanation.walkthrough: An online LSE would be an E-LSE, as with e-mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Else means other or different, as in 'someone else'.

clue.text: Game, but not golf, in deep shade

indicators.note: but not means the following letter is excluded from the word

parts.note: rugby is a ball game
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone plays a game other than golf in the shadows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shade' is a colour, not shadow.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruby is a deep rich red colour, named after the gemstone.

clue.text: Attack boys in blue suit

parts.note: a fit is a sudden attack, as of coughing
the Bill is British slang for the police, who wear blue uniforms

explanation.surface: Police officers being assaulted while in blue suits.
explanation.walkthrough: THE BILL is British slang for the police (also a long-running TV police drama).
explanation.definitionFit: To fit the bill is an idiom for being suitable, just what is needed.

clue.text: No tough guy, one's undesirable in bed

definitions.meaning: an unwanted plant in a garden bed

explanation.surface: A weakling dismissed as a poor lover.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is a flower bed, not a sleeping one.
explanation.definitionFit: Weed means both a weakling and an unwanted plant growing among cultivated ones.

clue.text: Figure entertaining both ladies and gents for free

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so this piece holds the other

parts.note: one is a number, a figure
Ladies and Gents are British names for public toilets, together the loos

explanation.surface: A celebrity offering free access to the public toilets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertaining' puts THE LOOS (Ladies and Gents being British labels for public toilets) inside ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: On the loose means at liberty, having escaped confinement.
